channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Advice for the new team
item.description: A satirical manifesto of advice to the newly elected Whitlam government, proposing new ministries for quality of life, gambling, sex, sport and protests, with nominations for permanent heads including George Moore, Germaine Greer and Barry Humphries.

item.title: Fun and gore on the Bazza set
item.description: Keith Dunstan watches the first day of filming of 'Barry McKenzie Holds His Own' at Palm Beach, where director Bruce Beresford orchestrates scores of blood-drenched extras and an imported CSIRO blowfly to create scenes of carnage on the beach and an idyllic barbecue beside Pittwater.

item.title: How to launch a custard pie
item.description: Pie-throwing at the Prime Minister during the Western Australian election campaign revives Keith Dunstan's interest in the history and technique of custard pie projection, with guidance from Mack Sennett's memoirs and Barry Humphries on why shaving cream beats actual custard for television.

item.title: Trams across the border
item.description: Sydney's consideration of re-introducing trams prompts Keith Dunstan to celebrate Melbourne's tram revival — a new $120,000 orange tram on Bourke Street, rising ridership for the first time in 20 years, and trams promoted as a tourist attraction — with Barry Humphries hosting a tram party to Wattle Park for a yellow-themed lunch, reciting his poem 'The Wattle Park Blues.'

item.title: The noble game on the big screen
item.description: With VFL attendance at its lowest since the war years and the ABC television series 'And the Big Men Fly' attracting protests over piled-on violence, Stoney Creek Films launches a $250,000 adaptation of Barry Oakley's 'A Salute to the Great McCarthy' — with Barry Humphries as club president Colonel Ball Miller — including a stunt requiring John Jarrat to leap from a seven-storey building in South Yarra.

item.title: Up there, Cazaly (10 points daily)
item.description: The Broadcasting Control Board's new Australian content points system throws an imagined commercial TV station into crisis, as its executives frantically try to squeeze poetry, literary criticism and ballet out of 81 hours of weekly football coverage, eventually hitting on a David Williamson sex-and-football drama combining 'Number 96' with the MCG.

item.title: Have you been asked lately?
item.description: As the 1975 federal election approaches, Keith Dunstan notices that unlike previous elections — when everyone from academics to kangaroo lovers signed full-page newspaper advertisements — nobody has asked him to sign anything this time, and he proposes organising 999 alderpersons and artists to publish their voting intentions in the Australian.

item.title: The dentist turned crusader
item.description: Alan Russell, a Maroochydore dentist who gave up his practice to become a full-time moral crusader, runs a printing press, campaigns against pornography and regularly telegrams politicians, representing a tradition of passionate individual protest that Keith Dunstan finds both admirable and exasperating.

item.title: Horsetrader Henry
item.description: A review of Peter Blazey's political biography of Henry Bolte, noting the dearth of Victorian state political biography and assessing Blazey's account of the premier's press management strategy, his brusqueness in cabinet, and the agony surrounding the hanging of Ronald Ryan.

item.title: Oh to be in Australia now that Al's there
item.description: Al Grassby's push to attract 250,000 expatriate Australians home inspires Keith Dunstan to propose a network of Australian Nostalgia Centres in London, Paris and New York, stocked with Fosters, Four 'n' Twenty pies, footy replays and Violet Crumble Bars.

item.title: The horror game
item.description: A visit to the former Melbourne Gaol after its transfer to the National Trust, where new displays of death masks, four skulls including Ned Kelly's, and the execution platform have elevated Melbourne's horror tourism above the Tower of London, though the authenticity of the Kelly skull remains disputed.

item.title: The big statue wrap-up
item.description: Inspired by Max Beerbohm's idea of covering London's statues rather than unveiling new ones, Keith Dunstan proposes a programme of veiling ceremonies for Sydney's pompous colonial bronzes, beginning with the dumpy Queen Victoria near the Supreme Court and moving on to Captain Cook, Captain Arthur Phillip and the weather-checking King Edward VII.

item.title: Cobber dobbers in Sunstroke Strip
item.description: Melbourne's second water crisis in five years has produced a new community phenomenon, the neighbour who rats on illegal waterers, garden bore-sinking at $1200 a pop, and a booming trade in plastic buckets and rubber bath-water diverters, prompting Keith Dunstan to suggest the city rebrand as Sunstroke Strip.

item.title: Sliding into corruption
item.description: A formerly clean-minded journalist surveys his local newsagent's paperback rack, finds 197 of 300 covers show bared women, reads a Number 96 tie-in novel's breathless prose, and concludes that sex has killed off the wholesome Western, and that only cleverly promoted immorality in Westerns could save it.

item.title: Through a tramcar window
item.description: The Metropolitan Tramways Board's plan to replace Melbourne's beloved old trams with 100 smooth, silent modern vehicles alarms Keith Dunstan, who proposes instead to have Ronald Searle or Bruce Petty design a nostalgic cast-iron beauty, with tourist trams running to Toorak and St Kilda complete with velvet seats and mahogany bars.

item.title: Full steam ahead for GM-H boss
item.description: Bill Gibbs, managing director of General Motors-Holden and new chairman of the loss-making Victorian Railways, should take a lesson from Echuca, where the annual steam and traction rally assembles entire squadrons of vintage Fowler steam engines, a steam pipe-organ and an eight-ton 1924 Sentinel steam truck whose party trick is tipping in three directions.

item.title: If marriage were abolished
item.description: The Whitlam government's proposed divorce reforms prompt Keith Dunstan to calculate the social and economic consequences of marriage's abolition, from confused dinner party seating and turbulent social pages through to the collapse of the wedding photography and reception industry and the ruin of jewellers.

item.title: We're all so delighted, obviously
item.description: Princess Anne's engagement to Lieutenant Mark Phillips revives Keith Dunstan's memories of covering Princess Margaret's engagement in 1960, when every newspaper deployed the word "obviously" to imagine royal feelings, Collins Street jewellers had replica engagement rings on display within days, and correspondents speculated the honeymoon must obviously be in Australia.

item.title: Glories of the site office
item.description: The twin-tower Collins Place project in Melbourne has built a $140,000 architect's site office so magnificent, with cathedral archways, 32 offices, PABX switchboards and pocket radios, that Keith Dunstan argues the city should forget the towers and simply lease the offices at $10 a square foot.

item.title: Eata bitta breada day
item.description: Amid the great diet bore of 1973, with 235 household diets in two years and Henry Bolte's grapefruit causing an Israeli fortune, the bread manufacturers fight back with a six-slices-a-day diet launched in the rain at Caulfield railway station with Ron Barassi present, though Keith Dunstan suggests the real PR solution would be spreading a rumour that wholemeal bread is the most potent aphrodisiac known to mankind.

item.title: Rubbishing the brochure fiends
item.description: Keith Dunstan proposes a Cram device, a combination rubbish bin and letterbox with a ball-bearing swivel allowing one swift flick to tip the entire morning's mail into the rubbish, as a remedy for the flood of direct mail targeting newly engaged, newly expecting and house-building households with everything from medieval-themed wedding menus to bronze-dipped baby booties.

item.title: Tasmanian sin needs a fair go
item.description: Every time Tasmania pioneers a decently sinful enterprise, the other states steal it, from the Tattersalls lottery to off-course betting to 10 o'clock closing, and now Wrest Point is offering Australia's first legal two-up but hesitating over who to appoint as ringmaster, while New South Wales threatens to legalise gambling houses and claim the sin capital mantle.

item.title: Captain Cook's cottage in sad decline
item.description: Melbourne's Captain Cook's Cottage, acquired in 1933 when philanthropist Russell Grimwade bought and shipped the Yorkshire house to Fitzroy Gardens, has risen from third to possibly first among the city's tourist attractions in the nostalgia wave, but The Age has now reported grimy walls, a leaking roof and water-drenched furniture, leaving the cottage due for a complete updating.

item.title: What we need is a virile virus
item.description: A survey of 17 years of newspaper virus vogues reveals a progression from Asian flu to Echo 6, American flu, Russian flu, Hong Kong flu and now London flu, and Keith Dunstan proposes that Australia should stake its own claim on the 1974 flu season by naming it the Whitlam grippe, boosting the prime minister's international profile while capitalising on 19th-century nostalgia.

item.title: Too late into nostalgia
item.description: Keith Dunstan's five-year-old business plan for Batman Atmosphere Laboratories, to mass-produce antique-look decor items from Greek columns to plastic cast-iron lacework, has been comprehensively beaten to market, with firms already selling machine-made antique bricks, fibreglass castles and miniature Waterloo cannons at $500 apiece.

item.title: Suffocated by awful anthems
item.description: Whitlam's national anthem competition produces terrible entries dominated by the words "God save," "Gough," and odes to nickel mines, but Keith Dunstan argues the best solution is to make Australia unique as the one country in the world that inflicts no national anthem on its subjects, since making 'Waltzing Matilda' official would ruin it forever.

item.title: A new weapon in the beer war
item.description: Courage Brewery's latest gambit in its disappointing campaign against Carlton is to put Brownlow Medal contenders' faces on aluminium cans, but after $5 million in accumulated losses and a series of failed products from Crest to Colonial Ale to Tankard beer, Keith Dunstan suggests they would do better decorating cans with writers, since almost all great Australian writers drink awfully well.

item.title: Now it's back to square one
item.description: Melbourne's decades-long city square saga returns to its starting point when English finance company Star Holdings collapses with over a million dollars in losses, meaning the Regent Theatre need never have closed, Hilliers' chocolate shop need never have shut, and the battle to save the Regent is on again, prompted by a letter from Barry Humphries of Canterbury.

item.title: Get rid of that (beep) telephone
item.description: The PMG's new 50-mile range paging device prompts Keith Dunstan to declare a pox on the telephone and report with admiration on Gordon De'Lisle, the Melbourne businessman who retired to Buderim, Queensland and refused to have a telephone installed even when the PMG sent in a team and his refusal caused them to be stunned beyond belief.

item.title: Toward a more viable tax scene
item.description: Treasurer Crean's inflation problem could be solved by a cliche tax ranging from $50 for the return of "churching the old whore" to 25 cents for each "in fact," since Keith Dunstan's monitoring of Parliament and TV current affairs reveals an epidemic of "viable," "cogent," "in this area," "gut feeling" and the coming word "elan," with Senator Gair's "fleas on an old dog" worth another $50.
